title: Explore the Brain
description: A guided tour through every major structure of the human brain, from the outer cortex down to the brainstem.

steps.title: 1 · The Cerebrum
steps.body: Start with the biggest structure: the cerebrum. Its wrinkled surface, the cortex, is folded to pack more thinking tissue into a skull-sized space. Everything else on this tour sits inside or beneath it.

steps.title: 2 · Frontal Lobe — planning and control
steps.body: The frontmost lobe. It governs voluntary movement, planning, and impulse control — the reason frontal lobe damage can change someone's personality.

steps.title: 3 · Parietal Lobe — sensing space
steps.body: Just behind the frontal lobe. It processes touch and body position, and helps you understand where things are in space.

steps.title: 4 · Temporal Lobe — hearing and memory
steps.body: Below the lateral fissure. It handles hearing and language comprehension, and — importantly — contains the hippocampus, which you'll meet in a few steps.

steps.title: 5 · Occipital Lobe — vision
steps.body: At the very back of the brain. Nearly all visual processing starts here, in the primary visual cortex.

steps.title: 6 · Corpus Callosum — the bridge
steps.body: A thick band of white matter running through the middle of the brain, connecting the left and right hemispheres so they can share information constantly.

steps.title: 7 · Lateral Ventricle — the fluid highway
steps.body: One of a pair of C-shaped cavities inside each cerebral hemisphere. They produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), the clear fluid that cushions the whole brain — it also has a matching structure on the right side.

steps.title: 8 · Third Ventricle — a narrow gap
steps.body: A slim, midline cavity sitting between the two halves of the thalamus. It's next in line as CSF flows from the lateral ventricles toward the brainstem.

steps.title: 9 · Thalamus — the relay station
steps.body: Deep in the core of the brain. Almost every sense (except smell) passes through the thalamus on its way to the cortex — it also has a matching structure on the right side.

steps.title: 10 · Hypothalamus — the regulator
steps.body: Just below the thalamus. Small, but it controls temperature, hunger, thirst, and hormones by directing the pituitary gland.

steps.title: 11 · Hippocampus — making memories
steps.body: Curled inside the temporal lobe. This is where new long-term memories are formed — one of the first areas affected as Alzheimer's disease progresses.

steps.title: 12 · Amygdala — emotion and fear
steps.body: Right next to the hippocampus. It processes emotional reactions, especially fear and threat detection.

steps.title: 13 · Caudate Nucleus — shaping movement
steps.body: A C-shaped structure deep in the cerebrum. Along with the putamen, it forms the striatum, helping plan and smooth out voluntary movement and supporting habit learning.

steps.title: 14 · Putamen — movement's control dial
steps.body: Sits alongside the caudate nucleus as part of the basal ganglia. Together they fine-tune how movements are initiated and carried out.

steps.title: 15 · Globus Pallidus — the output gate
steps.body: Tucked medial to the putamen. It's the basal ganglia's main output, sending signals that either allow or suppress movement — part of the circuit disrupted in conditions like Parkinson's disease.

steps.title: 16 · Cerebellum — balance and coordination
steps.body: Tucked underneath the back of the cerebrum. Despite its small size it holds most of the brain's neurons, fine-tuning movement, balance, and motor learning.

steps.title: 17 · Fourth Ventricle — the last chamber
steps.body: Sits between the brainstem and the cerebellum. CSF passes through here on its way down toward the spinal cord.

steps.title: 18 · Brainstem — keeping you alive
steps.body: The stalk connecting the brain to the spinal cord. It controls breathing and heart rate — which is why brainstem injuries are uniquely life-threatening.
